steps.body: Padding matters most in subtraction: 5.2 − 1.47 has nothing in the hundredths column until 5.2 is written as 5.20.
steps.narration: Padding matters most in subtraction: 5.2 − 1.47 has nothing in the hundredths column until 5.2 is written as 5.20.

commonResults.feedback: 433 flipped the short columns instead of trading — 7 − 0 and 4 − 2 are not legal moves when the top is smaller.
A borrow reached the hundredths but the tenths column was never charged for passing it along.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Add column by column from the ones; when a column reaches 10 or more, trade and carry.
widget.successFeedback: 24,681 + 13,247 = 37,928 — the ones make 8 with a carry that the tens must include.

predict.reveal: The value is unchanged; the zero simply fills the column so the borrow has somewhere to land.

cml.actionGoal: Work in the smallest place the numbers use, then decide where the point belongs for g5dc pad.
invariants: A decimal is place value continued past the ones: computing in the smallest shared place turns g5dc pad into whole-number arithmetic, and the point's position records which place the digits landed in.
misconceptions: Right-aligning digits instead of the points, treating a trailing zero as a change in value, or losing count of the decimal places a product carries.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the point moved one place left, how many times smaller would the amount become?

widget.prompt: Subtracting 5.2 − 1.47, what does writing 5.2 as 5.20 do?

options.label: It gives the hundredths place a digit to subtract from, without changing the value
options.feedback: Correct — a trailing zero adds no amount, but it fills the column so the subtraction has somewhere to work.

options.label: It makes 5.2 larger
options.feedback: 5.20 and 5.2 are exactly equal; the zero adds no hundredths at all.

options.label: It rounds the number up
options.feedback: Nothing is rounded — the value is untouched, only the way it is written changes.

options.label: It is not allowed
options.feedback: It is standard practice, and it is what makes ragged-length subtraction workable.
